G9A01: Parallel line impedance is set by how far apart the wires are and how thick they are. Length and frequency don't change it.
G9A02: High SWR makes power travel the line more than once, so a lossy line loses more.
G9A04: Power reflects when the feed line impedance and the antenna feed point impedance differ.
G9A05: Coax loss goes up as frequency goes up.
G9A06: Feed line loss is given in decibels per 100 feet.
G9A07: No standing waves means the antenna's feed point impedance matches the feed line's characteristic impedance.
G9A08: A tuner at the transmitter only fixes what the transmitter sees. The feed line still runs at 5:1.
G9A09: SWR = bigger impedance over smaller: 200 / 50 = 4, so 4:1.
G9A11: A lossy line eats some of the reflected power before it gets back, so SWR at the input looks lower (better) than it really is.
G9B01: A random wire fed right at the rig puts RF current on the station equipment, which becomes part of the antenna.
G9B02: Sloping the radials downward raises a ground plane's feed point impedance toward 50 ohms.
G9B03: A vertical ground plane radiates equally in all compass directions: omnidirectional in azimuth.
G9B04: A dipole radiates broadside: a figure-eight at right angles to the wire, with nulls off the ends.
G9B05: A dipole less than 1/2 wavelength high sends most energy upward, so at high angles its pattern is almost omnidirectional.
G9B06: Ground radials go on the surface or just a few inches under it.
G9B07: As a dipole gets closer to the ground, its feed point impedance steadily drops.
G9B08: Moving the feed point from the center toward the end raises the impedance steadily (current falls, voltage rises).
G9B09: Horizontal antennas have lower ground losses than verticals, which need a good ground system.
G9B10: Half wave in feet = 468 / MHz = 468 / 14.25 = 32.8, about 33 feet.
G9B11: Half wave in feet = 468 / MHz = 468 / 3.55 = 131.8, about 132 feet.
G9B12: Quarter wave in feet = 234 / MHz = 234 / 28.5 = 8.2, about 8 feet.
G9C01: Larger-diameter elements widen a Yagi's bandwidth.
G9C02: The driven element is about 1/2 wavelength, like a dipole.
G9C03: Reflector longer, director shorter than the driven element.
G9C04: dBi compares to an isotropic source, dBd to a dipole. A dipole has 2.15 dBi, so dBi is 2.15 dB higher.
G9C05: A longer boom with more directors gives more gain.
G9C07: Front-to-back = power in the main lobe compared with power off the back.
G9C08: The main lobe is the direction of strongest radiation.
G9C09: Two stacked Yagis double the gain: about 3 dB more.
G9C10: Boom length, number of elements and element spacing all tune gain, front-to-back and SWR bandwidth. All of these.
G9C11: A beta or hairpin match is a shorted stub of line across the Yagi feed point to match its impedance.
G9C12: A gamma match attaches at the element's center, which is at zero voltage, so the element needn't be insulated from the boom.
G9D01: For NVIS, mount a horizontal dipole low, between 1/10 and 1/4 wavelength high, so it sends energy straight up.
G9D02: An end-fed half wave is fed at the end, where voltage is high and current low: very high impedance.
G9D03: A halo radiates equally around itself in the plane of the halo (like a horizontal omni).
G9D04: Traps switch sections of the antenna in and out by frequency, giving multiband operation.
G9D05: Stacking Yagis one above another narrows the main lobe in elevation (a lower, flatter beam).
G9D06: A log-periodic's big advantage is wide bandwidth.
G9D07: In a log-periodic, element length and spacing change logarithmically along the boom.
G9D08: A screwdriver antenna runs a motor to change its base loading coil's inductance.
G9D09: A Beverage is a long, low wire for directional receiving on MF and low HF.
G9D10: A small loop has its nulls broadside to the loop (at right angles to its plane).
G9D11: Multiband antennas resonate on many frequencies, so they reject harmonics poorly.
G9D12: A dipole hung from one center support with the ends drooping is an inverted V.
